extracted.intended_audience: USCIS adjudicators, immigration attorneys/practitioners, stakeholders, and members of the public interested in the DHS public charge rule
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory standards and interpretive guidance DHS uses to determine whether an applicant is likely at any time to become a public charge, including statutory factors, evidentiary rules, exclusions, and public charge bond procedures. The page is the preamble and response-to-comments for the final rule implementing those standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory Minimum Factors (age)
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether a noncitizen is likely at any time to become a public charge, DHS must at a minimum consider the noncitizen's age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Age is one of the statutory factors to be considered in the totality of the circumstances. It must be reflected in written denials and considered alongside other factors; DHS guidance to officers will discuss how age affects likelihood to become a public charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory Minimum Factors (health)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will consider the noncitizen's health as evidenced by a report of an immigration medical examination performed by a civil surgeon or panel physician where such examination is required in making public charge inadmissibility determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS will generally defer to the report of the examination unless there is evidence that the report is incomplete. Health is one of the statutory minimum factors and should be evaluated as part of the totality of the circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory Minimum Factors (family status)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will consider the noncitizen's family status as evidenced by the noncitizen's household size; 'household' is defined in 8 CFR 212.21(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Family status is evaluated via household size and composition. See the separate 'Definition of Household' rubric for how household is determined and what income is included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory Minimum Factors (assets, resources, and financial status)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will consider the noncitizen's assets, resources, and financial status as evidenced by the noncitizen's household's income, assets, and liabilities (excluding any income from public benefits listed in 8 CFR 212.21(b) and income or assets from illegal activities or sources such as proceeds from illegal gambling or drug sales).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider household-level income, assets, and liabilities. Exclude income from public benefits enumerated in regulation and unlawful-source income. Household income may include income provided to the household from non-household sources (e.g., alimony, child support). This factor is one part of the totality-of-the-circumstances analysis and is not dispositive alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory Minimum Factors (education and skills)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will consider the noncitizen's education and skills as evidenced by the noncitizen's degrees, certifications, licenses, skills obtained through work experience or educational programs, and educational certificates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate formal credentials and practical skills/experience that affect the noncitizen's ability to be self-sufficient. Use documentary evidence (degrees, certifications, licenses, training, documented skills).

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit of Support (Section 213A) consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: The consular officer or immigration officer may consider any Affidavit of Support Under Section 213A of the INA submitted on the applicant's behalf when determining whether the applicant is likely at any time to become a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where an affidavit is submitted and required, it must be considered as part of the totality-of-the-circumstances analysis and reflected in any written denial explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of current and/or past receipt of specified public benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will consider the noncitizen's current and/or past receipt of public benefits most indicative of primary dependence: specifically TANF; SSI; State, Tribal, territorial, or local cash benefit programs for income maintenance; and long-term institutionalization at government expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS will take into account amount, duration, and recency of such receipt. Past or current receipt of these benefits is not alone dispositive; it is evaluated within the totality of the circumstances and used as evidence of likelihood of becoming primarily dependent on government for subsistence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of certain public benefits from consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not consider receipt of, or certification or approval for future receipt of, public benefits not referenced in 8 CFR 212.21(b) or (c), such as SNAP or other nutrition programs, CHIP, Medicaid (other than for long-term use of institutional services under section 1905(a)), housing benefits, benefits related to immunizations or testing for communicable diseases, or other supplemental or special-purpose benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explicit exclusion narrows the set of benefits that can be used as evidence in public charge determinations, intended to avoid chilling effects and to exclude benefits less probative of primary dependence. The preamble explains the policy rationale and reliance on input from benefits-granting agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-consideration of benefits received during exempt status or waiver periods
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not consider public benefits received by a noncitizen during periods when the noncitizen was present in a status exempt from the public charge ground of inadmissibility, or for which the noncitizen received a waiver of public charge inadmissibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also excludes consideration of benefits received by persons made eligible by Congress for resettlement assistance, entitlement programs, and other benefits available to refugees even if not admitted under section 207. This limits adverse effects on discrete populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'household' for family status and assets/resources
rubrics_metrics.description: The noncitizen's household will include: the noncitizen; if physically residing with the noncitizen, the noncitizen's spouse, parents, unmarried siblings under 21 years of age, and children; any other individuals who are listed as dependents on the noncitizen's federal income tax return; and any other individuals who list the noncitizen as a dependent on their federal income tax return.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Household income includes income provided to the household from sources who are not members of the household (e.g., alimony, child support). The household definition is used primarily to evaluate family status and assets/resources factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition change: replacement of 'alien' terminology for forward-looking inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS replaced the term 'alien' with 'beneficiary' (for long-term institutionalization) and 'individual' (for receipt of public benefits) to clarify that the forward-looking nature of the public charge inquiry includes events occurring after the applicant is no longer an 'alien' as defined in the INA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology change is to clarify scope of inquiry (e.g., long-term institutionalization or receipt of cash assistance after admission/adjustment may be relevant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference to immigration medical examination reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an immigration medical examination is required, DHS will generally defer to the report of the examination prepared by a civil surgeon or panel physician unless there is evidence that the report is incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the medical exam report as primary health evidence in the public charge health-factor assessment; only question it if incomplete or inconsistent with other evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality of the circumstances standard and use of nonbinding empirical guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Public charge determinations are prospective determinations made 'in the opinion' of the immigration officer based on the totality of the noncitizen's circumstances. DHS will issue subregulatory guidance to inform, but not dictate, officers' determinations; such guidance will consider how statutory factors affect likelihood to become a public charge and will be based on empirical analysis of best-available data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance will identify a range of nonbinding considerations and can be updated to reflect new data. The rule permits officers discretion within a structured, evidence-informed framework; officers are trained professionals and adjudicators will be expected to specifically articulate reasons for adverse determinations and provide opportunity to respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that USCIS written denials articulate consideration and reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposed to require that all written denial decisions issued by USCIS to applicants reflect consideration of each statutory minimum factor, the Affidavit of Support Under Section 213A where required, and the noncitizen's current and/or past receipt of public benefits, and to specifically articulate the reasons for the officer's determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This administrative requirement is intended to promote fair, consistent adjudications and to give applicants clear notice of the bases for adverse decisions and an opportunity to respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration rules regarding assets/income from illegal activities and public benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will exclude from consideration income or assets from illegal activities or sources (such as proceeds from illegal gambling or drug sales), and will exclude income from public benefits listed in 8 CFR 212.21(b) when evaluating assets, resources, and financial status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such exclusions narrow the evidence pool for assets/resources and align the financial assessment with lawful and relevant income sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of amount, duration, and recency of benefit receipt
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating past or current receipt of public benefits, DHS will consider the amount, duration, and recency of such receipt as part of the totality-of-the-circumstances assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This nuanced approach avoids treating any single receipt of benefits as dispositive; longer, larger, or more recent receipts are more probative of primary dependence than minimal, short-term, or remote receipts.

rubrics_metrics.name: T nonimmigrant adjustment applicants excluded from public charge ground
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS clarified that T nonimmigrants seeking adjustment of status are not subject to the public charge ground of inadmissibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a targeted rulemaking carve-out reducing paperwork and waiver needs for this subpopulation (e.g., T nonimmigrants would no longer need to submit Form I-601 to seek a waiver solely for public charge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public charge bond rules: cancellation and breach conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Public charge bonds will be cancelled upon death, permanent departure, or naturalization of the immigrant provided the immigrant did not breach the bond by receiving public cash assistance for income maintenance or long-term institutionalization at government expense; USCIS may cancel a bond after the fifth anniversary if the immigrant files Form I-356 and USCIS finds no receipt of such benefits prior to that fifth anniversary; bond cancellation authority lies with USCIS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These procedural rules define when bonds end and protect against automatic cancellation where covered benefit receipt occurred. They also shift certain authorities to USCIS rather than district directors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public charge bond rules: acceptance, form, and amount
rubrics_metrics.description: USCIS may invite adjustment applicants who are inadmissible only under section 212(a)(4) and otherwise approvable to submit a public charge bond in USCIS' discretion; USCIS will set the bond amount and provide instructions for submission; for consular immigrant visa cases the consular officer will set the amount; regulations set a floor of not less than $1,000 and require USCIS to provide a receipt on a form designated by USCIS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USCIS will determine administrative processes (form and receipt) and bond amounts; invitations to post bonds are discretionary and intended to allow admission/adjustment despite inadmissibility on public charge grounds where appropriate.
